A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PO-MFL research. Their main text, equations, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix E report original synthetic experiments on constant-velocity, crossing-path and circular-motion systems, including sensitivity and convergence results.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F retain the synthetic experiments and add original Wikipedia traffic results in Figure 5 and Table 1.

M1.justification: The reported Langevin updates remove the auxiliary epsilon term, changing noise from sqrt(2 eta (tau + epsilon)) to sqrt(2 eta tau). Algorithm 1 displays a forward-Euler cost instead of the midpoint cost, although v2 explicitly retains midpoint discretization for constant-velocity experiments. The underlying PO-MFL framework remains.

E1.justification: v2 extends evaluation from synthetic motion systems to real Wikipedia traffic: three pages over 500 days, using a fully observed autoregressive setting. The original synthetic coverage remains; circular motion moves to Appendix F.2 rather than being removed.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator remains the fully observed MFL method, renamed FO-MFL in v2. The Wikipedia experiment extends this same comparison to new data; newly discussed related methods are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The Wikipedia experiment introduces whole-trajectory W2 evaluation in R500, whereas the existing synthetic quantitative summary averages marginal W2 distances. Its protocol filters traffic to 100–500 visits, estimates autoregressive coefficients from 30 trajectories, tests m = 3, 6, 15 particles and evaluates three sampled output trajectories. Existing synthetic settings are retained.

E4.justification: Table 1 adds a particle-count sensitivity comparison for Wikipedia. The velocity-convergence diagnostic is revised from v1 Figure 3 to v2 Figure 2, including different traces and a longer displayed population-convergence interval. Existing velocity, observation-count and temporal-sampling sensitivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 Table 1 introduces means and one-standard-deviation uncertainty over 100 MCMC trials for Wikipedia. v1 provides no corresponding repeated-trial uncertainty summaries. This does not establish repeated independent optimization runs or new uncertainty reporting for the retained synthetic results.

E6.justification: v2 adds real-data trajectory-distribution results: Table 1 reports PO-MFL/FO-MFL normalized W2 means of 1.01/1.61, 1.07/1.76 and 1.05/1.91 for m = 3, 6 and 15, respectively. These have no v1 counterpart. Velocity-convergence traces also change, while the principal synthetic findings remain.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.4 and its appendix restatement replace auxiliary-epsilon annealing with tau annealing; the revised proof retains inconsistent old F_epsilon references. Section 3.2 corrects the kernel-cost multiplier from delta-t to tau_i. v2 also adds entropic-OT duality background and a cited finite-particle bound, while retaining the consistency, observability and representer proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims about latent trajectory inference, PO-MFL and theoretical guarantees remain. The conclusion broadens the empirical contribution from synthetic motion examples to include autoregressive models, reflecting the new Wikipedia application.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly excludes drift recovery from its scope and explains how temporal couplings characterize individual dynamics beyond population marginals. It also clarifies that the Wikipedia example uses fully observed data to test the dynamics prior. The existing model-misspecification and observability limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, the Wikipedia source filename and page identifiers, and preprocessing and optimization settings, including scaling by 1/50 and a 250-iteration Sinkhorn cap. It adds runtime complexity, Wikipedia runtime information and explicit Sinkhorn pseudocode. Existing synthetic settings and hardware information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of Kim et al.'s collective inference, Ventre et al.'s branching model, and drift-learning work by Tong et al. and Hashimoto et al. It also adds OT and finite-particle references. These refine positioning while preserving the main relationship to Lavenant and Chizat.

P1.justification: v2 expands explanations of the observation model and trajectory-distribution objective, adopts FO-MFL terminology and author-year citations, and adds an OT background appendix. Circular motion is reorganized into Appendix F.2. The main section sequence and most existing exposition remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds Wikipedia Figure 5, Table 1 and Sinkhorn Algorithm 2, relocates existing figures, and rearranges the circular-motion panels in the appendix. Figure 1 rescales displayed ground-truth variance, and the convergence plot changes axes. Conference formatting and captions change, but most existing plots are retained.

improvement.justification: The real-data study, uncertainty reporting and code/data instructions improve empirical breadth and reproducibility. However, replacing epsilon with tau changes the annealing formulation without consistently updating Theorem E.2 and its proof. New Sinkhorn Algorithm 2 also references an uninitialized psi(0) and specifies multiplicative updates that do not enforce the required marginals. These empirical gains and mathematical/documentation problems prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
